questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: identify the balances that make up M1
questions.stem: A bank teller lists what one customer holds: 900 in paper currency, 2,000 in a checking account, and 1,500 in a savings account. Which balances count toward M1?

options.text: The 900 in paper currency plus the 2,000 checking balance
The 900 in paper currency plus the 1,500 savings balance
options.misconception: counts a savings balance as immediately spendable transaction money

options.text: The 2,000 checking balance plus the 1,500 savings balance
options.misconception: believes cash on hand sits outside the money stock entirely

options.text: The 1,500 savings balance alone, since paper notes are already spent
options.misconception: thinks a savings balance substitutes for currency inside M1

questions.explanation: M1 is currency held by the public plus checkable deposits, so 900 + 2,000 = 2,900 counts and the 1,500 savings balance belongs to the near-money tier of M2. The trap is that any balance sitting in a bank account feels spendable, but savings must be transferred first, and the trap in the other direction is treating paper currency as money already spent and therefore uncounted.
questions.hint: Ask which balance the customer can spend without a transfer first.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: state what M2 adds to M1
questions.stem: A payroll clerk wants the broadest standard measure of the liquid balances a worker's pay can become. Which combination is that measure?

options.text: M1 plus savings deposits, small time deposits, and money market funds
M1 plus currency sitting idle inside the central bank's own vault
options.misconception: counts the issuer's idle vault cash as part of the money stock

options.text: Checkable deposits plus gold bullion and corporate bond holdings
options.misconception: treats investment holdings as though they were money

options.text: M1 minus savings deposits, since saving destroys part of the money stock
options.misconception: believes M2 can be smaller than the M1 inside it

questions.explanation: M2 is M1 plus near-money: savings deposits, small time deposits, and money market fund shares, so M2 always exceeds M1. Bullion and corporate bonds are investments rather than money, and currency in the central bank's own vault has left circulation, so both are the standard overshoots. Subtracting savings would make M2 smaller than the M1 it contains, which can never happen.
questions.hint: Ask what the second tier of the money stock adds to the first.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: decide whether a credit card balance is money
questions.stem: A household carries a credit card with a 3,000 balance and a debit card drawing on 3,000 in checking. Which statement about the two balances is correct?

options.text: Only the checking balance is money; the card balance is a promise to repay
Both balances are money, since each one can buy goods the same day
options.misconception: counts credit card limits as spendable money today

options.text: Only the card balance is money, since it permits the larger purchase
options.misconception: believes borrowing capacity outranks cash holdings

options.text: Both balances are money, since each records an obligation of a bank
options.misconception: treats any recorded bank obligation as part of the stock

questions.explanation: Money settles a payment now, and a checking balance does that; a credit card balance is a promise of future payment, so it sits in neither M1 nor M2. The trap is that a card feels like spending power because it buys things today, but the purchase is settled later out of income, which is exactly why no money stock carries those balances.
questions.hint: Ask which balance settles today's payment without a promise attached.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why a bank can pay a deposit in full
questions.stem: A single bank holds 1,000 in vault cash against one 1,000 checking deposit, and the reserve requirement is 0.10. Why can it still pay out the full 1,000?

options.text: Because only a tenth of deposits must be held, the rest fund day-to-day payouts
Because the central bank clears every check without touching the vault
options.misconception: believes clearing removes the need for any payout reserves

options.text: Because required reserves are advisory guidance, not a legal obligation
options.misconception: treats the reserve requirement as a nonbinding suggestion

options.text: Because deposits are money only while they stay inside the banking system
options.misconception: thinks checkable balances stop counting once withdrawn

questions.explanation: A fractional reserve system requires only a slice of each deposit to sit idle, so a bank with 1,000 of deposits can hold 100 and still honor 1,000 of withdrawals by drawing on balances other customers left behind. The trap is that the vault looks like the account itself, but those notes are assets, while the 1,000 owed to the depositor is a liability payable in notes or in transfers.
questions.hint: Ask what share of the deposit the rule actually requires.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute M1 from a component list
questions.stem: Currency in circulation is 840 billion, traveler's checks outstanding are 16 billion, and checkable deposits total 2,144 billion. What is M1? Report the number only.
questions.explanation: M1 is the sum of its own three components: 840 + 16 + 2,144 = 3,000 billion. Adding savings deposits, which belong to M2, is the usual overshoot, and dropping traveler's checks, which the older definition still counts as checkable, is the usual undershoot.
questions.hint: Add only the components that sit in the narrowest measure.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the simple money multiplier as one over the reserve ratio
questions.stem: In a country where reserves are the only leak from the banking system, the required reserve ratio is 0.05. What is the simple money multiplier?

options.misconception: inverts the reserve ratio instead of taking its reciprocal
reports the reserve ratio itself rather than its reciprocal
adds one to the reciprocal, double counting the first deposit

questions.explanation: The simple multiplier is one divided by the reserve ratio, 1 / 0.05 = 20. It is called simple because it assumes every dollar lent comes straight back as a deposit, with currency and idle reserves ignored. Reading 0.05 as the answer confuses the ratio with its reciprocal, and 50 counts the very first deposit twice.
questions.hint: Invert the reserve ratio; do not multiply by it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a money stock from an income flow
questions.stem: An analyst reports that a country's M1 is larger than its national income for the year. Which correction is the right one?

options.text: M1 is a stock at a point in time, while income is a flow over a year
M1 is a yearly flow, while national income is a stock at year end
options.misconception: swaps the two and treats the money stock as annual income

options.text: Both figures are stocks, so only the units of measurement differ
options.misconception: believes accumulated income can be a point-in-time stock

options.text: M1 is a stock of paper notes, so it cannot be compared to anything
options.misconception: reduces M1 to physical currency and denies comparison

questions.explanation: A money stock is measured on a single date while national income accumulates across a year, so the comparison mixes a stock with a flow and can read as 'larger' for arithmetic reasons alone. Calling M1 a flow inflates it by a year's worth of turnover, and refusing to compare the two at all misses that they become comparable once put on the same time basis.
questions.hint: Ask whether each figure is measured on a date or accumulated over a period.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: apply the reserve requirement to the right deposit base
questions.stem: In a country with a 0.10 reserve requirement, a bank holds 2,000 in checkable deposits and 5,000 in savings deposits. Which base is the requirement applied to?

options.text: Checkable deposits only, since only those balances are payable on demand
Savings deposits only, since they pay the bank the higher rate
options.misconception: applies the requirement to the higher-rate liability

options.text: Both deposit types equally, since every account carries the same rule
options.misconception: assumes one rule covers every deposit product

options.text: Neither deposit type, since the rule applies to paper currency
options.misconception: reads the requirement as a rule about physical notes

questions.explanation: The requirement is written against checkable deposits, the balances payable on demand, so the base is 2,000 and required reserves are 200. Applying the ratio to savings instead gives 500, the trap that yields a 300 answer, and reading the rule as one about paper currency moves the base off deposits entirely.
questions.hint: Apply the ratio to the balances that must be payable immediately.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute required reserves from the deposit base
questions.stem: A bank holds checkable deposits of 6,000 and faces a required reserve ratio of 0.08. How many reserves must it hold against those deposits?
questions.explanation: Required reserves are the ratio applied to the deposit base, 0.08 x 6,000 = 480. Dividing instead of multiplying inverts the rule and gives 75,000, and the 5,520 left over once the requirement is set aside is the excess rather than the requirement itself.
questions.hint: Multiply the deposit base by the stated ratio.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute excess reserves from reserves held and required
questions.stem: A bank holds 640 in vault cash against deposits of 5,000, with a required reserve ratio of 0.10. What are its excess reserves?
questions.explanation: Required reserves are 0.10 x 5,000 = 500, so the excess is 640 - 500 = 140, the amount the bank can newly lend. Answering 500 gives the legal floor instead of the lendable surplus, and answering 640 treats every dollar of cash as spendable capacity when 500 of it is locked up.
questions.hint: Subtract the required amount from the reserves actually held.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: sum the first rounds of the deposit ladder
questions.stem: Reserves are the only leak and the required ratio is 0.20. A new 1,000 reserve deposit is relent in successive rounds. How much is lent in the first three rounds?
questions.explanation: Each round lends its own excess reserves, so the sequence runs 800, then 0.80 x 800 = 640, then 0.80 x 640 = 512, and 800 + 640 + 512 = 1,952. Stopping after two rounds gives 1,440, counting the first deposit as a lending round gives 2,952, and the 4,000 lent once the ladder runs out answers a different question.
questions.hint: Lend the excess reserves of each round, then add the three rounds.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: derive bank capital from the balance sheet identity
questions.stem: A bank's balance sheet lists loans of 5,000, vault cash of 1,200, and customer deposits of 5,400. Setting other items aside, what is the bank's capital?

options.misconception: nets deposits against loans instead of adding both to assets
reports vault cash as the residual left after liabilities
reports the total asset figure instead of the residual

questions.explanation: A balance sheet must balance, so assets equal liabilities plus capital: (5,000 + 1,200) - 5,400 = 800. Subtracting the loan figure from deposits, 5,400 - 5,000 = 400, nets a liability against an asset, and 6,200 is the asset total rather than what is left for the owners.
questions.hint: Add the assets, subtract the liabilities, and the rest is capital.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute net interest income from lending and deposit rates
questions.stem: A bank earns 9 percent on 600 million in loans and pays 4 percent on 500 million in deposits, with no other interest items. What is its net interest income, in millions?
questions.explanation: Interest income is 0.09 x 600 = 54 and interest expense is 0.04 x 500 = 20, so net interest income is 54 - 20 = 34. Adding the two to get 74 treats interest paid as income, and pairing 9 percent with the 500 deposit base gives 45, which prices the liability at the lending rate.
questions.hint: Compute the income and the expense separately, then subtract.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the money multiplier as M1 over the monetary base
questions.stem: A central bank reports currency in circulation of 1,200 and reserve balances of 800, so the monetary base is 2,000. If M1 stands at 5,000, what is the money multiplier?
questions.explanation: The money multiplier is the money stock divided by the monetary base that supports it, 5,000 / 2,000 = 2.5. Reversing the division returns 0.4, which claims the stock is smaller than its own base, and 2,000 is the base itself rather than the multiple of it.
questions.hint: Divide the money stock by the base that supports it.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: classify customer deposits on a bank balance sheet
questions.stem: A bank teller points to a balance sheet line reading 4,000 in customer checking balances. Why does that line sit on the liabilities side?

options.text: The bank owes those balances to depositors, who hold claims against it
Deposits are assets, because depositors hold a claim on the funds
options.misconception: flips the claim so the depositor owes the bank

options.text: The line is a liability, because deposits are taxed as bank income
options.misconception: explains the classification with a tax rule

options.text: The line is a liability, because reserves are owed to depositors
options.misconception: credits depositors with a claim on reserves

questions.explanation: A liability is money the bank must pay out on demand, and a checking balance is exactly that, so the 4,000 sits opposite assets such as loans and cash. The trap is that depositors feel they own the balance, but the legal claim runs from the depositor to the bank, which is why the vault holds reserves rather than their deposits.
questions.hint: Ask who owes whom at the moment the customer withdraws.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: place currency in circulation on the central bank balance sheet
questions.stem: On a central bank's balance sheet, where does the currency sitting in the pockets of the public appear?

options.text: As a liability, because the central bank issued those notes and owes claims
As an asset, because the notes store value for whoever holds them
options.misconception: credits the issuer with the public's store of value

options.text: As an asset, because the public's notes back the central bank's gold
options.misconception: pairs circulating notes with the issuer's gold stock

options.text: Nowhere, because currency in circulation is an off-balance-sheet item
options.misconception: removes a recorded obligation from the statement

questions.explanation: Currency in circulation is issued by the central bank and redeemable on demand, so the public's claim is a liability of the issuer, just as reserves are a liability owed to banks. Calling it an asset reverses who owes whom, and pairing it with gold confuses a liability owed by the central bank with an asset it holds.
questions.hint: Ask whether the public or the central bank is the party owing.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: exclude the issuer's own vault cash from the monetary base
questions.stem: A central bank's own vault holds 40 billion in paper currency. Where does that stack sit in the monetary base?

options.text: Outside the base, which counts currency in circulation and reserve balances
Inside the base, because the notes are already printed and issued
options.misconception: counts currency as money from the moment of printing

options.text: Inside the base, counted as reserve balances owed to deposit banks
options.misconception: reclassifies idle notes as reserves held by banks

options.text: Counted twice, once as currency in circulation and once as reserves
options.misconception: double counts a single stack across both base components

questions.explanation: The base is currency in circulation plus reserve balances, and notes sitting in the issuer's own vault are neither, because nobody outside the bank holds them as a claim. The trap is that printed notes look like money the moment they exist, but the base counts only the ones the public and the banks can actually spend.
questions.hint: Ask whether anyone outside the central bank holds a claim on those notes.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: record the two sides of a central bank asset purchase
questions.stem: A central bank buys 3,000 of government bonds and credits the seller's account at another bank. Which pair of central bank entries follows?

options.text: Bonds rise 3,000 and reserve balances rise by the same 3,000
Bonds rise 3,000 and currency in circulation rises 3,000
options.misconception: credits the public with notes instead of bank reserves

options.text: Reserve balances rise 3,000 while total central bank assets fall
options.misconception: reads a liability payout as a loss of central bank assets

options.text: Currency in circulation falls 3,000 while reserve balances rise
options.misconception: has a completed purchase shrink the note stock on hand

questions.explanation: Paying for the bonds credits the seller's reserve account, so assets rise by the 3,000 of bonds and liabilities rise by the 3,000 of reserves; on a central bank balance sheet one side never moves alone. Crediting currency instead of reserves misreads what the payment settles, and treating the reserve payout as a drop in total assets confuses a liability with a loss.
questions.hint: One side of the central bank's balance sheet must rise for the other.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: apply the money multiplier with currency and excess-reserve leaks
questions.stem: The public holds 20 percent of any deposit expansion as currency, banks hold 10 percent of deposits as extra reserves, and the required ratio is 0.10. What is the money multiplier?

options.misconception: uses the simple one over the required ratio, ignoring both leaks
inverts the fraction, putting the denominator over the numerator
forgets the extra reserve term in the denominator

questions.explanation: With a currency ratio of 0.20, extra reserves of 0.10 and a required 0.10, the multiplier is (1 + c) / (r + e + c) = 1.20 / 0.40 = 3.0. Ten is the simple 1 / 0.10 that pretends reserves are the only leak, 12 drops the extra reserve term from the denominator, and 0.33 inverts the ratio.
questions.hint: Put currency in the numerator and all three leaks in the denominator.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: convert a deposit multiplier into a money multiplier
questions.stem: A deposit multiplier of 4 holds in a country, but the public keeps 25 percent of every new deposit as currency. What is the money multiplier?

options.misconception: reports the deposit multiplier and ignores the currency held
subtracts the currency share instead of adding it to one
answers with the currency ratio and never multiplies it

questions.explanation: Each dollar of new reserves ends as 4 dollars of deposits plus 1 dollar of currency, because 0.25 of 4 is 1, so broad money rises by 4 x 1.25 = 5.0. Reporting 4.0 keeps the deposit multiplier, subtracting the currency share gives 3.0, and 1.25 is the currency ratio on its own with no deposit multiplier attached.
questions.hint: Find the currency created per deposit, then add it to the deposits.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish one bank's capacity from system-wide creation
questions.stem: A single bank takes a 900 deposit and holds the required 0.10 with no extra reserves. Can that one bank on its own create deposits by lending the excess 810?

options.text: No, one bank lends only its own excess reserves; the system expands
Yes, that bank alone can lift deposits to 9,000 by relending
options.misconception: confuses the system multiplier with a per-bank entitlement

options.text: No, banks may lend only deposits received from other customers
options.misconception: thinks a fresh deposit is not lendable at all

options.text: Yes, because the reserve requirement applies to currency, not deposits
options.misconception: moves the requirement off deposits to make lending free

questions.explanation: A single bank can lend its 810 of excess reserves, and that loan creates one 810 deposit at that bank; expansion beyond it needs the borrower's payment to land in some other bank, which then lends in turn. So the multiplier is a whole-system result, and one bank claiming ten times its own deposit has confused a system ratio with a per-bank rate.
questions.hint: Follow where the borrowed money gets deposited next.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain that a requirement change posts no balance sheet entry
questions.stem: A regulator cuts the required reserve ratio from 0.10 to 0.05 overnight, and banks held no excess reserves the day before. What changes on their balance sheets immediately?

options.text: Nothing at first, because a rule change moves no reserves off the books
Reserves fall at once, as banks must hand the freed cash to the regulator
options.misconception: invents a payment that a rule change never makes

options.text: Deposits shrink, since older balances no longer meet the new rule
options.misconception: makes grandfathered balances instantly noncompliant

options.text: Loans double at once, as every deposit can now be lent twice over
options.misconception: reads a halved ratio as a doubled lendable share

questions.explanation: A reserve requirement is a rule about future behavior, not a transaction, so no reserve account moves on the day it changes; it only frees capacity for the loans and deposits that follow. Treating it as a release of cash invents a payment that never happened, and halving the ratio does not double the lendable share of a deposit.
questions.hint: Ask whether any entry was posted, or only the rule changed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why the observed multiplier falls short of one over the required ratio
questions.stem: A country sets its required reserve ratio at 0.10, yet the measured money multiplier is 1.6 rather than 10. Which explanation best fits that gap?

options.text: Banks hold spare reserves and the public holds currency, both draining the base
Banks must park the full 10 percent in cash for every deposit taken
options.misconception: inverts the gap by treating the floor as the whole story

options.text: The required ratio applies to currency but never to checkable deposits
options.misconception: moves the requirement to the wrong balance to explain it

options.text: Banks are barred from lending more than reserves received that day
options.misconception: claims a legal one-day cap on every individual loan

questions.explanation: The simple 10 assumes every lent dollar returns as a deposit; in practice banks keep a cushion above the requirement and the public hoards part of each expansion as cash, so the real multiplier is (1 + c) / (r + e + c) and lands well under 10. Treating the requirement as the whole story inverts the gap, since holding exactly 10 percent is the floor, not the reason the measured figure is smaller.
questions.hint: Name the two things that stop a deposit from being lent again.

questions.learningObjective: read the monetary base off a central bank statement
questions.stem: A central bank lists assets of 5,200 in government bonds, 100 in discount loans, and 300 in other assets, against liabilities of 2,000 currency in circulation, 3,000 reserve balances, and 600 other liabilities. What is the monetary base?

options.text: Reserve balances plus currency in circulation, which total 5,000
Government bonds plus currency in circulation, which total 7,200
options.misconception: counts a central bank asset as part of the base

options.text: Other assets plus other liabilities, which total 900
options.misconception: reads the residual lines as though they were the base

options.text: Discount loans plus reserve balances, which total 3,100
options.misconception: mixes a central bank asset with a bank liability

Bonds are an asset the central bank chose to hold, not a base component, and pairing discount loans with reserves mixes the issuer's asset with a liability owed to banks.

questions.learningObjective: sort balance sheet lines into assets and liabilities
questions.stem: A bank's balance sheet lists vault cash 500, loans to customers 4,000, customer deposits 3,600, and long-term bonds 900. Which pair are both assets of the bank?

Vault cash and customer deposits, both held on customers' behalf
options.misconception: puts the owed balance on the side the bank owns

options.text: Customer deposits and loans, both funded by the bank's owners
options.misconception: claims deposited money came from bank capital

options.text: Loans and customer deposits, both claims the bank holds
options.misconception: calls an owed balance a claim the bank holds

The trap is the 3,600 of customer deposits, which belong on the liabilities side because the bank owes them, and pairing a liability with an asset is the error most students make here.

questions.learningObjective: use excess reserves to compare two banks' lending capacity

Both banks, because 4,000 of deposits supports 40,000 of loans
options.misconception: applies the system multiplier to each bank alone

options.text: Only the first bank, because 400 of reserves meets the requirement
options.misconception: treats meeting the requirement as lending capacity

options.text: Neither bank, because the requirement is set above any legal holding
options.misconception: claims the stated ratio is impossible to satisfy

Running the multiplier bank by bank to reach 40,000 treats a system-wide ratio as a per-bank entitlement that each bank can draw on by itself.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: correct the belief that re-lending one deposit creates new money
questions.stem: A student argues that the 1,000 sitting in a bank vault is the same money reappearing in every later loan, so banks never create anything new. What is the flaw?

options.text: Each loan credits a fresh deposit while the vault money stays where it is
Nothing is wrong; bank loans simply pass the same cash along
options.misconception: denies that a loan can create a deposit

options.text: The flaw is that banks may not earn any interest on deposits
options.misconception: redirection to an interest rule about deposits

options.text: The flaw is that vault cash must be insured before any loan is written
options.misconception: claims deposit insurance is a precondition for lending

questions.explanation: A loan is a new liability created against the bank, so the borrower's deposit is new money even though the vault cash never moves, and that new deposit then funds the next loan. Counting the same 1,000 in every round double counts it, and the ceiling of 1 over the reserve ratio limits new deposits, not the number of times old cash is re-lent.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: explain why clearing a check between banks creates no money
questions.stem: A customer writes a 500 check drawn on Bank A, and the payee deposits it in Bank B, which holds the required 0.10 and no extra reserves. Explain what happens to total checkable deposits across the two banks.

answer.exemplar: Bank A's deposits fall by 500 and Bank B's deposits rise by 500, so system deposits are unchanged, because a payment moves an existing claim rather than making a new one. Reserves never leave the two banks, and Bank B's only new lending capacity is the 450 of excess reserves the deposit creates there: 500 of new reserves less the 50 it must hold.

questions.explanation: A payment reallocates an existing deposit: reserves stay inside the two banks and the deposit total simply changes hands, so the money stock is untouched by the check itself. Creation requires a new loan, and 500 of fresh deposits at B against a 0.10 requirement leaves B with 500 - 50 = 450 of excess, which is the only new lending this event makes possible.
questions.hint: Separate a claim that changes hands from a claim that is newly created.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: read a shift between M1 and near-money in a report
questions.stem: A quarterly report shows M1 falling from 1,200 to 1,150 while M2 rises from 3,400 to 3,460, so near-money grows by 110. Which reading best fits those numbers?

options.text: Balances shifted out of checkable accounts into savings and money market funds
Checkable deposits shrank because households hoarded far more paper currency
options.misconception: calls currency a flight out of M1 when it sits inside

options.text: The money multiplier fell, so each unit of reserves created less money
options.misconception: blames a slower multiplier for two measures moving apart

options.text: Banks broke their reserve requirements and were forced to shrink deposits
options.misconception: invents a rule violation to explain the composition

questions.explanation: M2 minus M1 is near-money, and it grew from 2,200 to 2,310, so 110 moved into savings and fund shares while 50 left transaction balances: that is a portfolio shift between tiers of the same stock. Currency is itself part of M1, so hoarding would lift M1 rather than cut it, and a lower multiplier would shrink both measures instead of pulling them apart.
questions.hint: Compute M2 minus M1 in each period and see which tier grew.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: correct the belief that lending out deposits creates payout reserves
questions.stem: During a run, a bank treasurer argues that lending out every new deposit is safe, because each new loan leaves the bank holding fresh reserves to meet withdrawals. What is the flaw?

options.text: A loan creates a deposit owed to the borrower, not a reserve to the bank
Nothing is wrong; every new loan leaves the bank holding new reserves
options.misconception: insists lending always adds spendable reserves on hand

options.text: The flaw is that reserve requirements rise automatically during a run
options.misconception: claims the legal ratio tightens on its own

options.text: The flaw is that the central bank can lend only against government bonds
options.misconception: restricts central bank lending to one kind of collateral

questions.explanation: When a bank lends it credits the borrower's deposit and books the loan as an asset, so reserves are unchanged while liabilities grow, and reserves arrive only when someone pays in rather than when someone borrows. That asymmetry is why a solvent bank under fractional reserves can still be forced to sell assets under withdrawals, which is why deposit insurance and a lender of last resort exist.
questions.hint: Check which account a loan credits: a liability or a reserve.
